name: Bahrain
summary_text: Bahrain is a place to avoid entirely, but with the thinnest active-enforcement record in the Gulf. Uniquely among Gulf states, same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1976, and there is no statute criminalising transgender expression. The UK foreign office notes "arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare." However, broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions are used against gender and sexual minorities — penalties include imprisonment, fines, and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a Manama hotel discotheque on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A Brazilian trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite a female passport marker. In 2023 a court rejected a trans man's recognition application citing Islamic Sharia, and in February 2024 the lower house of parliament adopted a bill to criminalise "acts of deviance" — a deteriorating trajectory. For a visitor: the legal exposure is real but enforcement is sporadic; the modal risk is indecency arrest followed by deportation rather than imprisonment.

sources.claim_summary: Wikipedia overview: same-sex sexual activity decriminalised in Bahrain since 1976; gender identity recognition 'limited'; no discrimination protections, no relationship recognition, no LGBT-inclusive family rights. Sections cover enforcement incidents, false accusations, and derogatory terminology.

sources.title: Bahrain: Continued Denial of Legal Gender Recognition and Gender-affirming Healthcare for Transgender People in the Name of Islamic Sharia | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 analysis (Feb 2024): in May 2023 a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia - despite extensive medical documentation from Bahrain and abroad. The court cited Sharia to deny both healthcare and recognition.

sources.title: Bahrain | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 country review of Bahrain: independent human-rights researchers and advocates (including UN bodies and Amnesty) have long been denied entry or research access, so local media are the main source on trans arrests and legal details are scarce. Laws are used to punish gender non-conformity; discriminatory violence by state and non-state actors is widely reported; trans people are denied gender-affirming healthcare (intersex people are permitted medical transition).

sources.title: Bahrain | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Bahrain decriminalised same-sex relations in 1976 and is the only Gulf state not explicitly penalising same-sex intimacy - but authorities use 'indecency'/'debauchery' provisions to arrest queer and trans people. A February 2024 bill criminalising 'acts of deviance' with a person of the same sex and its 'promotion' had not passed into law as of March 2026. No LGBTIQ organisations operate; a 2023 court denied a trans man's gender-marker change, echoing a 2016 ruling.

sources.title: Responses to Information Requests - Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada
sources.claim_summary: Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, Response to Information Request BHR105575.E (2016): 'Bahrain: Situation of sexual minorities, including societal attitudes and treatment by authorities (2011–July 2016)'.

Pride Source (Jan 2010): 'Cross-dressers arrested in Bahrain' — nine cross-dressers of various Arab nationalities arrested at a Manama hotel discotheque on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery.

English translation of Bahrain's Penal Code 1976 (MENA Rights Group): the full criminal code text - includes the morality provisions (Articles 324-325 'outraging public decency' and related offences) used against gender-nonconforming people, though same-sex conduct itself is not explicitly criminalised.

al-bab blog (Dec 2014): 'Too gay to represent Bahrain' - discusses the Muftah collection on LGBTQ sexualities in the Middle East, including the case of a Bahraini perceived as too gay to represent the country; broadens analysis beyond simple persecution narratives.
